transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten completely out of hand, and I don't really know how it happened so fast. I'm an artist, you see, and normally I have a pretty good rhythm with my work, but lately, I've just been... well, I've been taking on everything. I mean, *everything*. I started this massive new mural project downtown, which is a huge commitment on its own, but then I also agreed to teach three new advanced painting workshops at the community center, which means I have to write all the syllabi and gather materials for thirty students. And on top of that, I decided this was the perfect time to completely renovate my studio space—I’ve been tearing out the drywall myself, trying to put in better skylights because the natural light just hasn't been right for my recent color palettes. 

And then there are the client calls. I’ve been scheduling consultations back-to-back, sometimes double-booking myself, promising these elaborate commission pieces with ridiculously short turnaround times. I just felt so full of energy, like I could finally do it all, you know? Like the ideas were just flowing and I had to catch them all before they disappeared. But now... now I’m looking at the calendar, and the deadlines are all piling up, overlapping in this terrifying way. The studio is a complete disaster zone, half-finished, and I haven't even started on the commissions I promised by the end of the month. The mortgage is due, and I’ve spent so much on the renovation supplies and workshop materials that I’m stretched completely thin. It’s like the walls are literally and figuratively closing in on me, and I just... I can't keep up with the pace I set for myself. I really thought I could handle it all, but now I'm just drowning in it.
Did you feel unusually energetic when you decided to take on all these new projects?

Oh, energetic doesn't even begin to cover it, doctor. It was like... like I had swallowed a lightning bolt, or maybe like there was this constant, low-level electric hum just vibrating right through my bones, from the very second I opened my eyes in the morning. Usually, I need a good hour and a half, maybe two cups of dark roast coffee just to feel human, but during this time? No. I was just *up* and instantly moving. I’d be out of bed before the sun was even properly up, and the energy was so intense that just sitting still, just taking a breath, felt physically uncomfortable. It felt almost impossible, honestly. So I just kept moving. I would start rearranging the entire layout of the studio—hauling heavy canvases, dragging the drafting tables across the room because I suddenly decided the Feng Shui was blocking my creative flow. And while I was doing that, I’d be mentally drafting these huge, ambitious grant proposals for public art installations, and the second I put down a piece of furniture, I'd be on my laptop, firing off emails to gallery owners, city council members, former clients, just anyone who popped into my head. And then I'd be right back up, fussing with all my supplies, sorting hundreds of tubes of oil paint by color family and then by brand, just because I couldn't stop my hands from moving. It was this relentless, driving need to *do* something, constantly, because the energy inside me was just so loud and so fast.
Did you find yourself needing less sleep than usual during this highly energetic period?

Sleep? Oh, sleep was... well, it's hard to even call it sleep, honestly. It was more like a very brief pause in the action. I wasn't really *needing* it, if that makes sense. I mean, usually, I'm the kind of person who absolutely has to get my full eight hours. If I get seven and a half, I'm sluggish, my brushstrokes are sloppy, my eyes just won't focus on the finer details of a piece. I need that restorative time, you know? But during those weeks, it was like my body just forgot how to be tired. 

I would be in the studio until maybe three, sometimes four in the morning, just covered in plaster dust and paint, completely wired. And then I'd think, 'Okay, I should probably lie down, just because that's what people do.' So I'd go upstairs, wash my hands—which took forever because I was trying to get all the gesso out from under my fingernails—and I'd get into bed. But my mind would just keep racing, spinning out these elaborate color theories and planning out the exact dimensions for the community center syllabi. I'd maybe doze off for an hour, maybe two? And then, boom. My eyes would snap open. It wasn't a groggy wake-up either; it was instant clarity. Instant readiness. I'd look at the clock, see it was 5:15 AM, and instead of groaning and rolling over, I'd just throw the covers off and think, 'Right, time to tear down that east wall!' 

And the strangest part, doctor, is that I didn't feel exhausted the next day. Not at all. I felt invincible. I was running on maybe ninety minutes of sleep, day after day, for weeks, and I felt more awake than I ever have in my entire life. I kept telling my friends—the few I actually had time to talk to—that I had finally unlocked some secret human potential, that sleep was just this unnecessary biological habit we'd all been brainwashed into needing. It sounds absurd now, saying it out loud, but at the time, I truly believed I just didn't require rest anymore. I just kept pushing and pushing, fueled by whatever that electric feeling was.
Did you find yourself feeling extremely happy or irritable at any point during this highly energetic period?

Well, it was... it was a mix of both, honestly, but in this very extreme way. Most days, I just felt... oh, unusually buoyant. Like I was literally floating above the ground. I felt lit up from the inside, you know? Like every single thing in my life, the studio renovations, the mural, even my garden out back—I had started ripping up the azaleas to put in this elaborate, multi-tiered fountain system—it was all just finally clicking into place. I felt this profound sense of joy and purpose, like the universe was just handing me the keys to everything. I'd be humming while I was covered in drywall dust, just so completely, wonderfully happy. 

But then... well, then there was the other side of it. Because I was moving so fast and I had this perfect, crystal-clear vision of how everything was supposed to go, if anyone—and I mean *anyone*—got in my way or slowed me down, I would just... snap. And I don't mean just getting a little annoyed. I mean I would snap sharply, like a whip. My assistant, bless her, she tried to ask me about some unpaid invoices from the workshop materials, just a simple, practical question, and I absolutely lost it on her. I started yelling about how she was interrupting my creative flow, how she was dragging me down into mundane details when I was trying to build a legacy. I told her she lacked vision and basically kicked her out of the studio for the day. And the contractors I hired to help with the skylights? If they told me something wasn't structurally possible, I'd get so incredibly irritable, just furious that they couldn't see what I was seeing. I'd argue with them for hours, pacing around the room, telling them they were incompetent. It was like... if you were on my wavelength, everything was beautiful and euphoric, but the second you questioned my plans or tried to pull me back to reality, I became this completely different, incredibly harsh person. It's embarrassing to think about now, how I spoke to people, but at the time, their hesitation just felt like a physical roadblock I had to smash through.
Did you ever hear voices or see things that weren't there during this time when you felt so energetic?

Voices or seeing things... well, you know, it’s complicated, doctor. Because when you're in that state, when the energy is just humming through your bones and the studio is covered in plaster dust and you haven't really slept in days, your senses get so... heightened. Almost distorted, really. Every sound is magnified, every shadow looks a little too sharp. 

But what really took over my mind—what was far more intense and disruptive than just seeing a shadow move out of the corner of my eye—was this absolute, undeniable paranoia I developed. It was just this overwhelming conviction about my clients. You have to understand, in the fine art world, your ideas are your currency. If someone takes your concept for a public installation or copies your specific technique, they're essentially taking your livelihood. So, sure, before this, I might worry about contracts, I’d make sure my NDAs were signed and my copyrights were filed, just standard professional diligence. But I didn’t believe people were plotting against me. 

Not until this happened, anyway. That certainty about clients stealing my work only showed up during this keyed-up stretch with the studio. I mean, I was convinced, entirely and completely convinced, that my collectors and gallery owners were secretly coordinating with each other, trying to get a look at my new canvases, trying to steal my exact color mixing formulas before I could debut the collection. I was literally covering the new skylights with heavy canvas tarps because I thought they had hired people to watch me work from the roof! I was locking my sketchbooks in a fireproof safe every time I walked into the kitchen for a glass of water. It was exhausting, this constant, buzzing feeling of being under surveillance by the very people who were supposed to be supporting my career. 

And as for the hallucinations you asked about... well, if my mind was playing visual tricks on me or if I was hearing whispers in the hum of the drafting lamps, it was entirely confined to that one, massive surge of energy. I haven’t had voices or visions outside of this period. Before the studio renovations and after I finally crashed, there was absolutely nothing like that. It was all just locked into that one, terrifyingly intense stretch of time where my brain was just running completely out of my control.
How long did this highly energetic period last?

How long... well, time is such a strange thing to measure when you're moving that fast, isn't it? It felt like a decade, honestly, but if I really look at the calendar and trace it back to the exact starting point... it's been going on for about three months. 

Yes, three months. I can pinpoint it exactly because it all started right around the time I took on the mortgage for the cottage-studio. I had been searching for a dedicated workspace for years—something with proper northern exposure, you know, because the light in my old space was just dreadful for mixing oils, everything always looked too warm. And when this little cottage came on the market, I just knew I had to have it. The closing process was an absolute nightmare, just endless paperwork and back-and-forth with the bank, but the day I finally signed those papers and officially took on that mortgage... it was like a switch flipped. A starter pistol just went off in my brain. 

So from that day forward, it was just three solid months of this relentless, buzzing momentum. Ninety days of tearing down walls, ripping up the azaleas, arguing with contractors, hiding my canvases from everyone... I mean, three months might not sound like a massive chunk of time in the grand scheme of a fifty-four-year life, but when you are living every single second of it at absolute maximum velocity, it feels like an eternity. Just... an entire season of my life swallowed whole by that electric feeling. It's staggering to look back and realize I sustained that pace for a full quarter of the year.
Have you felt a return to your normal energy levels since this three-month period ended?

Return to my normal energy levels... well, that's the thing, isn't it? What is normal anymore? I mean, I suppose the short answer is no, I haven't. But it's not like I just smoothly transitioned back to the way I was before I bought the cottage. It's more like... like I was driving a sports car at a hundred and fifty miles an hour for three months straight, and then suddenly, the engine just completely seized up. 

I didn't just go back to my baseline, doctor. I crashed. I mean, I hit a wall so hard I'm still feeling the bruises. After all that time of barely sleeping, of tearing down walls and painting until my fingers cramped, of being so incredibly vigilant about my clients spying on me... one morning, I just woke up and the electricity was gone. The buzzing in my bones just stopped. And what was left behind was just this heavy, hollow exhaustion. 

I look at the studio now, with the half-finished fountain and the tarps still over the skylights, and I don't feel any of that joy or purpose I was telling you about. I just feel overwhelmed. I can barely muster the energy to mix a single palette, let alone finish the collection. Getting out of bed feels like I'm wearing a lead suit. So, no, I wouldn't call this normal. I don't feel like myself at all. I just feel... depleted. Like I spent a decade's worth of energy in ninety days, and now my account is completely overdrawn. It's just so stark, the contrast between how I felt then and how I feel right this very second. I just want to feel like me again, you know? Not the hurricane I was, and not this... this puddle I am now. Just me.
Are you still experiencing significant fluctuations in your energy levels?

Fluctuations? Well, since the crash... since that engine seized up like I was saying, it hasn't really been fluctuating so much as just staying incredibly low. I mean, I suppose there are moments, tiny little blips where I think, "Oh, maybe I'll go out to the studio and just... just organize the brushes," but by the time I actually put my shoes on, that thought is completely gone and I'm just sitting on the edge of the bed staring at the floorboards. 

So it's not like I'm bouncing back and forth between that wild, electric hurricane feeling and this heavy, lead-suit feeling. It's just... it's just the lead suit now. Every single day. I wake up, and I think about the mortgage on that cottage, and I think about the galleries expecting new work, and it just presses me further down into the mattress. There's no buzzing, no momentum, no... no sudden urge to rip up the azaleas again. It's just this flat, gray, exhausting stillness. I haven't had any of those high-energy days since the crash happened. It's just been a very steady, very deep low.
Are there any days where you feel slightly better than others since the crash?

Slightly better? I mean... I suppose there are degrees to the exhaustion, aren't there? It's not always exactly the same shade of gray, if you want to look at it that way. But "better" feels like much too strong a word. 

Some days... well, some days I can manage to make a pot of coffee instead of just drinking tap water, or I might actually walk out to the mailbox at the end of the driveway. Yesterday, for instance, the sun was hitting the kitchen window just right—it's this lovely, warm afternoon light that usually makes me want to sketch—and for about ten minutes, I actually felt a tiny fraction lighter. I thought, "Maybe I'll just go sit on the porch." I didn't actually do it, of course. I just sat at the kitchen table looking at the dust motes in the air. But the thought was there. 

But then there are the other days, the really bad ones, where even the thought of making coffee feels like I'm being asked to climb a mountain in the snow. Those are the days where I just pull the covers over my head and ignore the phone ringing. My sister has been calling constantly, worried sick, I'm sure, but I just... I can't. I can't explain this to her. I can't explain how I went from building a fountain in the middle of the night to not being able to pick up a ringing telephone. 

So, yes, I suppose there are very, very minor fluctuations in just how heavy the lead suit feels on any given day. A little less crushing on Tuesday, maybe a little more suffocating on Thursday. But none of it approaches "better." None of it feels like I'm actually climbing out of the hole. It's just... shifting around at the bottom of it, trying to find a slightly less uncomfortable position in the dirt. Does that make sense? It's all just variations of the same terrible, depleting low.
Have you experienced any feelings of worthlessness or guilt since your energy levels crashed?

Worthlessness or guilt... well, I don't know if I'd use those exact words, but... actually, no, I wouldn't. I mean, I certainly feel awful about the state of things. I look at the studio, and I see the mess I made, the half-finished projects, the tarps, the money I spent on that cottage... and it's overwhelming. It's frustrating. I feel stupid for having done all of that, for getting so carried away, but... I don't sit here thinking I'm a worthless person, if that's what you mean. 

I'm just so tired. The exhaustion is so loud, it kind of drowns everything else out. I know I should feel guilty about not answering my sister's calls, because she's just trying to help, and I know I'm probably worrying her sick. And the galleries... I mean, they were expecting the new collection, and I haven't even looked at an email in weeks. But it's not a deep, agonizing guilt that keeps me up at night. It's more just... a dull awareness that I'm letting people down, and I just don't have the energy to care enough to fix it. 

I suppose when I was in the middle of it all, when I was tearing down the walls and convinced my clients were watching me, I felt incredibly important. Like everything I was doing was vital. Now, I just feel empty. But not worthless. Just... like a shell that used to have something inside it. I don't know if that's the same thing as what you're asking. It's just so hard to muster up any strong emotion, even guilt, when just breathing feels like a chore. I just want to sleep, doctor. I just want to close my eyes and not have to think about the cottage, or the paintings, or any of it.
Have you ever felt this low or experienced a similar crash in energy and mood before this incident?

Have I ever felt this low before? No... no, I really don't think I have. I mean, I'm an artist, so of course I've had periods of melancholy over the years. You don't get through a fine arts graduate program without a few existential crises, right? I remember back in my thirties, I had a gallery show that completely flopped—just terrible reviews, the lighting was all wrong, hardly anyone bought anything—and I spent about a week and a half in my pajamas just eating dry toast and crying. But that was... that was just disappointment. It was circumstantial, you know? It was sad, but it wasn't this. 

This feels entirely different. It's not a reaction to a bad review or a creative block. It's like the actual machinery inside my body and my brain has just completely broken down. Before this whole thing... before the cottage and the fountain and that intense, buzzing electric feeling where I thought I was creating my absolute masterpiece... I had a pretty steady rhythm to my life. I'd work, I'd rest. Sometimes I'd work a little too late into the night if the inspiration struck, sure, but I always bounced back the next morning. 

But this crash... it's like falling off a cliff instead of just tripping on the sidewalk. I've never gone from feeling so incredibly invincible, so completely dialed into the universe, to just... nothing. Absolutely nothing. It's completely uncharted territory for me. I think that's partly why it's so paralyzing, even though I don't even have the energy to properly feel the panic of it. I'm just sort of vaguely aware that this isn't normal for me. 

So, no, I've never been in a hole this deep or this dark before. I've never had my energy just evaporate like this. It's a completely new experience, and... and I really just don't know how to navigate it. I don't know how to get back to whatever my normal used to be.
Are you currently feeling hopeless about your future?

Hopeless? I... I don't know if "hopeless" is the right word, exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting here thinking my life is completely over and I'll never pick up a paintbrush again. I don't have this dramatic, sweeping vision of a ruined future. It's more just... a complete inability to picture the future at all right now. 

When you're this exhausted, when just getting up to get a glass of water feels like a monumental task, the idea of "the future" is just too big. It's too heavy. I can't think about next month, or next year, or even next week. I can barely think about tomorrow morning. So I wouldn't say I'm filled with despair about what's coming, because I'm not really looking that far ahead. 

It's just this dense fog, you know? Like I'm stuck in this thick, gray soup, and I can't see more than an inch in front of my face. I'm not exactly hopeless, but I'm definitely not hopeful either, because hope requires energy. Hope requires you to imagine something better, and I just... I don't have the mental bandwidth for that right now. I'm just trying to get through the next hour, the next minute, really. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm actively hopeless. I'm just incredibly, profoundly stuck in the present moment, and the present moment happens to be very, very tiring. I just want to rest. I don't want to think about the future, or the past, or the cottage, or the galleries. I just want to close my eyes and not have to exist quite so loudly for a little while.
Have you ever experienced another period in your life where you had a similar high-energy phase followed by a crash?

Another high-energy phase followed by a crash? No, no, I... I don't think so. I mean, I really can't recall anything quite like what just happened with the cottage and the fountain and then this... this absolute void I'm in now. 

I've always been a passionate person, you know? You have to be, in my line of work. When I'm working on a new collection, I get very focused. I might work late into the night, maybe skip a meal here or there because I'm just so absorbed in the colors, the textures, the way the light hits the canvas. I remember back in my twenties, right after grad school, I was doing this series of large-scale abstracts, and I'd stay up until three or four in the morning for a few days straight just painting. I felt energized by the work, certainly. But that was just... that was just the creative process. It was inspiration. It wasn't this frantic, electric buzzing where I felt like I was receiving messages from the universe or... or tearing down walls because I thought people were watching me. 

And the crashes after those periods of intense work? They were just normal exhaustion. I'd finish a big project, ship it off to the gallery, and then I'd sleep for twelve hours and spend a couple of days watching old movies and eating takeout. It was a recovery period, a very natural winding down. It wasn't this... this complete collapse of my entire being where I can't even fathom getting out of bed to brush my teeth. 

So, no, I've never experienced anything of this magnitude before. Not the extreme high, and definitely not this... this suffocating low. It's all entirely new, and frankly, it's terrifying, even though I'm too tired to really feel the terror. Does that make sense? It's just... it's never been like this. Never.
Have you ever had another episode like this in your past, where you experienced a high-energy phase followed by a crash?

I... wait, didn't we just go over this? Or maybe I'm losing my mind a little bit more than I thought, I'm sorry. My brain is just moving through molasses right now, everything is blurring together. 

But, um, no. Like I was just saying, I really haven't. If I had ever experienced a crash like this, or a high like that, I... I really think I would have remembered it. Or someone else would have noticed! My ex-husband, for example. We were married for fifteen years, all through my thirties and into my early forties, and he was always very... well, very observant about my habits. He used to joke about my "painting frenzies" when I'd drink way too much espresso and leave my dirty brushes in the kitchen sink for days because I was so focused on a canvas. But that was just normal artist eccentricity, you know? Just getting lost in the work. 

He never, ever had to deal with me thinking the universe was sending me secret messages, or... or find me completely paralyzed in bed for days afterward, unable to even lift my head off the pillow. If anything even remotely like this had happened back then, he would have dragged me to a doctor immediately. He was very practical, very grounded like that. 

So I can say with absolute certainty that this is the very first time my brain has ever done... whatever it is it's doing right now. I keep trying to comb through my past, trying to find some precedent for it, maybe thinking back to my time in London or my early gallery days, searching for some clue that this was always inside me, but... nothing. There's nothing. It's just a completely unprecedented disaster.
Have you ever had another time in your life where you felt as invincible and full of energy as you did during the three months before your crash?

Invincible... that's a very specific word, isn't it? And, I know we've been circling around this same topic for the last few minutes, but to address that specific feeling... no. Never. I have never felt invincible before those three months. 

I mean, what does it even mean to feel invincible normally? When I was in my thirties, I had this very successful solo exhibition. The reviews were glowing, pieces were selling before the doors even officially opened, and I felt on top of the world. I felt confident, I felt validated, I felt like a very successful, very happy human being. But I still knew I was human. I still knew I had to eat, and sleep, and pay my taxes, and that if I fell down the stairs I would break a leg. 

But those three months before this... this awful fog rolled in? It was entirely different. It wasn't just confidence. It was this absolute, undeniable certainty that the normal rules of physics and biology just didn't apply to me anymore. I genuinely felt like my blood was carbonated, like I was made of pure electricity or light. I'd be out there at the cottage, hauling heavy stones for that fountain at two in the morning, and my muscles wouldn't even ache. I didn't feel pain, I didn't feel fatigue. I felt like I could have stopped a moving car with my bare hands if I wanted to. 

So, to keep answering the question... no. I have never, ever experienced anything even close to that level of invincibility or energy in my entire fifty-four years on this earth. It was a complete anomaly. And frankly, looking back on it from... from this heavy, gray place I'm in right now, it's exhausting just remembering it. I don't know how my physical body actually survived running at that speed for that long. But no, there is no other time in my past that compares to it. Not one. I'm sure of it.
Did you make any impulsive decisions during the three months when you felt incredibly energetic?

Impulsive? Oh, God, yes. Impulsive is... well, impulsive feels like an understatement, to be honest. It wasn't just a whim here or there, it was this absolute, overwhelming compulsion to act immediately on every single idea that flashed into my brain, because every idea felt like a revelation. 

I was at the cottage, right? And I had this vision for a completely new direction in my work—this massive, multimedia, immersive installation. And instead of, you know, sketching it out, making a budget, maybe talking to my gallery director like a rational fifty-four-year-old professional, I just... I just started buying things. I bought this enormous, top-of-the-line, large-format archival printer. We're talking thousands and thousands of dollars, just put right on the credit card without a second thought. And then I needed the right paper, of course, so I ordered crates of this imported, handmade specialty paper from Japan and Italy. 

And then I looked at the cottage studio and decided the lighting was all wrong for what I was about to create. So I didn't just buy a few lamps; I went out and bought thousands of dollars in high-end track lighting, daylight bulbs, and then—this is where it gets really crazy—I started buying renovation materials. Lumber, drywall, expensive hardware, because I suddenly decided I needed to knock out a wall and completely rebuild the interior of the studio myself to accommodate the printer and the new lighting. 

I was just swiping my card, signing invoices, completely convinced that it didn't matter what it cost. I honestly believed that this project was going to be my magnum opus, that it was going to change the art world, and that the money would just... sort itself out. I thought the universe would provide, or the gallery would advance me a fortune once they saw the genius of it. I didn't even look at my bank balances. It wasn't until the crash happened, until this awful fog settled in and I couldn't even get out of bed, that I finally looked at the statements. And... and it's terrifying. I spent so much. I put the cottage, my studio, my entire financial stability in so much jeopardy. I was so close to real, irreversible trouble, and I couldn't even see it while it was happening. I just kept buying and buying and building and building...
Did you experience any psychotic symptoms, such as delusions or hallucinations, during the three-month period when you felt incredibly energetic?

Psychotic... gosh, that's such a frightening word to hear applied to yourself. It makes me feel... well, it makes me feel very small just hearing it. As for hallucinations, like seeing things that aren't there or hearing voices? No, nothing like that. My eyes and ears were working just fine. But... if you mean believing things that weren't real? Then, yes. I suppose I did. 

I... I know it sounds extreme, especially now that I'm sitting here in this heavy, slow state of mind, but during those months, I became absolutely certain that people were trying to steal my ideas. Because of that massive installation I was telling you about, I was developing this entirely new technique, this whole complex system of layering the imported paper with the archival prints. I thought it was revolutionary. And I got it into my head that a couple of my clients—people who have collected my work for over a decade, people I normally trust implicitly—and even this one editor from an arts magazine I've known for years, were all trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the system. 

I mean, they would send me what I now realize were totally normal emails. Just asking how my time at the cottage was going, or wondering if I had any new pieces in the works. But back then? I would read those emails and my heart would just pound out of my chest. I read between the lines of every single word. I thought they were fishing for information, trying to scoop my idea and give it to another artist, or publish it before I was ready. I actually started hiding my sketchbooks inside the oven when I wasn't actively drawing in them. Can you imagine? A fifty-four-year-old woman hiding books in an oven. 

And the worst part is, I confronted them about it. I sent these awful, cryptic, defensive emails telling them to back off and that my intellectual property was protected. They were so confused. They tried to tell me, over and over, that they were just checking in, that they were just being supportive friends and colleagues, but... it didn't matter. No amount of reassurance from them really settled me. I would just nod along on the phone and then immediately go back to thinking they were lying to my face. I just couldn't shake this profound, terrifying conviction that I was being hunted for my ideas. It’s just... it’s so deeply embarrassing to admit now, how completely I lost the plot. I don't even know how I'm going to look those people in the eye again.
Are you currently experiencing a depressed mood or a loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed?

Depressed? Um... no, I really wouldn't say that. I know I used the word 'fog' earlier, and I said things felt heavy right now, but I want to be really clear about what that means, because 'depressed' sounds like... well, it sounds like crying all day in the dark or feeling completely hopeless about the world, and that’s just not what’s happening with me. 

The heaviness I mentioned is really just the sheer physical and mental exhaustion of coming down from running at a hundred miles an hour for three months. It's like my internal battery is just completely, utterly drained, but my mood itself isn't actually sad or down. I'm just tired. Very, very tired from the adrenaline leaving my system. 

And as for losing interest in things? Oh, absolutely not. Never. Art is my entire life. Even with all the financial stress and the profound embarrassment with my colleagues that I was just telling you about, I still want to create. I was actually just out in the studio yesterday morning, looking at all those crates of imported Japanese paper I bought. And even though I was kicking myself for how much it all cost, I was still running my hands over the texture of the sheets, still imagining how the archival ink is going to look when it absorbs into the fibers. I still have all the passion for my work, even if I have to scale the project back to reality. 

I still love my other hobbies, too. I spent two hours on Sunday pruning the hydrangeas at the cottage, which I always enjoy, and I've been reading a lot. So, no, I haven't lost interest in the things that bring me joy, and I really wouldn't call my mood depressed. I'm just dealing with the aftermath, you know? I'm just trying to sweep up the massive mess I made while I was so full of electricity, but the core of who I am and the things I love doing haven't changed at all.
Are your energy levels stable now?

Stable? Well, I suppose 'stable' is one way to put it, though like I said a moment ago, 'depleted' or 'grounded' might be a bit closer to the reality of right now. But if you're comparing it to how I was during those three months? Oh, absolutely. It is night and day.
